name: Republic of Vietnam
info: The anti-communist state of southern Vietnam, proclaimed by Ngô Đình Diệm in 1955 after the partition at the 17th parallel, which fought the Vietnam War with American support until the fall of Saigon in 1975.

facts.founder: Ngô Đình Diệm, who declared himself president on 26 October 1955 after the referendum of 23 October
facts.predecessor: State of Vietnam (1949–1955), an associated state within the French Union under Bảo Đại
facts.successor: Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam (1975), merged into the Socialist Republic of Vietnam on 2 July 1976

t: After the 1954 Geneva Conference divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, the State of Vietnam ruled the South, and in October 1955 a referendum widely marred by fraud deposed Bảo Đại and made Ngô Đình Diệm president of the new republic.

Diệm's authoritarian rule under the doctrine of Personalism ended in the Buddhist crisis and his killing in a US-backed coup in 1963; after four years of military juntas, the 1967 constitution opened the Second Republic under Nguyễn Văn Thiệu.

At the Paris Peace Accords of 1973 South Vietnam fielded about one and one-half million troops, but after US forces withdrew and aid was cut, the North's conventional invasion of 1975 ended with Dương Văn Minh's unconditional surrender on 30 April.
dyk: In the referendum of 1955 that made Diệm president, over 380,000 more votes were cast than there were registered voters, and in Saigon he was credited with 133% of the vote; his American advisers had recommended a more modest margin of 60 to 70 percent.
ev: Ngô Đình Diệm's referendum removes Bảo Đại as head of state, and on 26 October Diệm declares himself president of the Republic of Vietnam
The Huế Phật Đản shootings of 8 May set off the Buddhist crisis, and on 1 November Diệm is overthrown and killed in a coup led by General Dương Văn Minh
A new constitution creates a bicameral legislature, and Nguyễn Văn Thiệu is elected president with 34% of the vote in a widely criticised poll
The People's Army of Vietnam and the Việt Cộng launch the Tet Offensive, which fails militarily but marks a turning point in US support
The government begins the Land-to-the-Tiller program of land reform, limiting individual landholdings to 15 hectares
The Paris Peace Accords are signed on 27 January, and US military forces leave South Vietnam at the end of March
Thiệu announces that the war has restarted, and China attacks South Vietnamese forces in the Paracel Islands and takes control of them
Communist forces overrun Saigon, and President Dương Văn Minh surrenders South Vietnam unconditionally on 30 April

sections.foundation:
The Republic of Vietnam grew out of the State of Vietnam, created on 14 June 1949 through co-operation between anti-communist Vietnamese and the French during the First Indochina War, with the former emperor Bảo Đại as chief of state. After the 1954 Geneva Conference divided Vietnam temporarily at the 17th parallel, the State of Vietnam administered the territory to the south, which took in the southern and part of the central regions of the country. About one million people moved South during the period of relocation, among them at least 500,000 Catholics and about 200,000 Buddhists, while about 90,000 Việt Minh were evacuated to the North.

Ngô Đình Diệm, prime minister since 1954, held a referendum on 23 October 1955 asking voters to approve a republic and so remove Bảo Đại. The poll, supervised by his younger brother Ngô Đình Nhu, credited Diệm with 98 percent of the votes. On 26 October 1955 Diệm declared himself president of the newly proclaimed Republic of Vietnam, with its capital at Saigon. He had announced in July 1955 that South Vietnam would not take part in the elections specified in the Geneva Accords, and in December 1955 he ended the economic and financial agreements with France; the French, who needed troops in Algeria, had completely withdrawn by April 1956.
sections.socioeconomy:
South Vietnam kept a capitalist free-market economy with ties to the West, greatly assisted by American aid and by the presence of large numbers of Americans between 1961 and 1973. Between 1954 and 1973 electrical production increased fourteen-fold, industrial output rose by an average of 6.9 percent a year, rice output by 203 percent, and the number of university students from 2,000 to 90,000. Diệm's land reform of October 1956 limited rice farms to 247 acres per landowner but had stalled by 1960, since many of his biggest supporters were large landowners; the Land-to-the-Tiller program of 1970 limited holdings to 15 hectares.

In 1968 the population was estimated at 16,259,334, though about one-fifth of the people of the Mekong–Dong Nai delta lived in areas controlled by the Viet Cong. In 1970 about 90% were Kinh and 10% Hoa, Montagnard, Khmer, Cham, Eurasians and others. Between 3 and 4 million people were Buddhists, the Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo religions had between 2.5 and 3 million followers, and about 10% of the population was Catholic. From 1955 the Diệm government pursued an assimilation policy towards the Montagnard and the Cham, banning the Cham language in public schools and seizing indigenous lands for Kinh settlers.
sections.military:
The Republic of Vietnam Military Forces were formally established on 30 December 1955 from the French-led Vietnamese National Army, itself gathered in July 1951 from colonial auxiliary units, and comprised the Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN), the Air Force, the Navy and the Marine Division. Conscription began in 1957, though its enforcement was lax. The French ceased training the forces in 1956, and American advisers restructured them along US lines; the country was divided into four corps tactical zones and the Capital Military District around Saigon.

The insurgency of the Viet Cong, armed and supported by North Vietnam, had by 1961 brought half the rural region south and southwest of Saigon under considerable communist control, by a US intelligence estimate. American combat troops arrived in 1965, and during the Tet Offensive of February 1968 over a million South Vietnamese soldiers served beside 500,000 US soldiers and 100,000 from allies such as South Korea, Australia and Thailand. The invasion of Laos in 1971 was defeated by the PAVN, and the North's conventional invasion of 1972 was repulsed only with massive US air support. In 1973 the state fielded the fourth largest military force in the world, but it depended on the US for spare parts, fuel and ammunition.
sections.governance:
South Vietnam was a unitary and centralised state whose politics moved from authoritarianism under the ideology of personalism (1955–1963) to fractious military juntas (1963–1967) and then to the Second Republic (1967–1975). Diệm adopted Personalism, a doctrine presented as a third way between Marxist collectivism and Western capitalism, gave key posts to his family, with Ngô Đình Nhu gaining authority over the military, police and intelligence, and built a personality cult through the Ministry of Information and Youth and the National Revolutionary Movement. US representatives reported that his government regularly ordered the execution of political opponents and shut down dissident newspapers, and peasants were forcibly relocated into "strategic hamlets".

After a series of coups, Air Marshal Nguyễn Cao Kỳ became prime minister in 1965 with General Nguyễn Văn Thiệu as figurehead chief of state. The constitution of 1967 granted freedom of speech, press and association and created a House of Representatives and a Senate. Thiệu won the presidency in elections widely considered fraudulent and was re-elected unopposed in 1971 with 94% of the vote, his rule growing more dictatorial. Amnesty International in 1973 put the number of civilian prisoners at 35,257 to 200,000 or more. The country was divided into forty-four provinces.
sections.impact:
South Vietnam belonged to the Western Bloc and was a close ally of the United States, which saw it as a counterbalance to communist North Vietnam. Its sovereignty was recognised by 95 countries as of January 1975, but its admission to the United Nations was vetoed by the Soviet Union; it held observer status at the General Assembly and belonged to the World Health Organization, UNESCO, the World Bank, the IMF and other agencies. Its defence drew the United States into the Vietnam War on a large scale from 1965, and the Tet Offensive of 1968 led the Nixon administration to the policy of Vietnamization.

Within the country Buddhists, Catholics, students, labour unions and a non-government press formed a fragmented but active civil society. The historian Peter Zinoman sets a productive intellectual and cultural life and a republican political culture beside the regime's authoritarianism, militarism and dependency on the US, and the 'Vietnamese turn' scholarship of recent decades has challenged earlier portrayals that dwelt on its negative side. The assimilation policy in the Central Highlands fed movements such as FULRO, which fought both South Vietnam and the succeeding Socialist Republic of Vietnam until the late 1980s.
sections.decline:
Under the Paris Peace Accords of 27 January 1973, US forces left at the end of March 1973 while PAVN forces in the South remained in place. The Case–Church Amendment of 4 June 1973 prohibited renewed American intervention, the oil price shock of October 1973 brought inflation that left the government struggling to pay its soldiers, and in August 1974 Congress cut aid from $1 billion a year to $700 million. Thiệu declared on 4 January 1974 that the war had restarted, and the same month China took the Paracel Islands. Phuoc Long, abandoned in early January 1975, was the first provincial capital to fall.

The offensive at Ban Me Thuot opened the Ho Chi Minh Campaign. Thiệu's withdrawal from the Central Highlands became a rout, Huế and Da Nang were captured, and by early April the PAVN had overrun almost three fifths of the South. After a last-ditch defence by the ARVN 18th Division at the Battle of Xuân Lộc, Thiệu resigned on 21 April and fled to Taiwan; Trần Văn Hương held office for a week before the assembly handed the presidency to Dương Văn Minh, who surrendered unconditionally on 30 April 1975. The Provisional Revolutionary Government then became the government of the South, which merged with the North on 2 July 1976, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

summary: The Republic of Vietnam was the anti-communist state of southern Vietnam from 1955 to 1975. Born of the partition of 1954 and dependent on American aid and arms, it passed from Diệm's personalist dictatorship through military juntas to the Second Republic, and fell to the North's invasion in April 1975.
references: Edward Miller, Misalliance: Ngo Dinh Diem, the United States, and the Fate of South Vietnam (Harvard University Press, 2013)
Jessica M. Chapman, Cauldron of Resistance: Ngo Dinh Diem, the United States, and 1950s Southern Vietnam (Cornell University Press, 2013)
Nu-Anh Tran, Disunion: Anticommunist Nationalism and the Making of the Republic of Vietnam (University of Hawaiʻi Press, 2022)
Van Nguyen-Marshall, Between War and the State: Civil Society in South Vietnam, 1954–1975 (Cornell University Press, 2023)
Christopher Goscha, Vietnam: A New History (Basic Books, 2016)
Heather Marie Stur, Saigon at War: South Vietnam and the Global Sixties (Cambridge University Press, 2020)

pointDescs.1955: A rigged referendum removes Bảo Đại, and Ngô Đình Diệm proclaims himself president of the Republic of Vietnam on 26 October.
pointDescs.1956: The French complete their withdrawal by April, and Diệm launches a land reform program in October.
pointDescs.1959: North Vietnam's Communist Party approves a "people's war" on the South, and Group 559 is set up to maintain the Ho Chi Minh trail.
pointDescs.1961: A US intelligence estimate reports that half the rural region south and southwest of Saigon is under considerable communist control.
pointDescs.1963: The Buddhist crisis follows the Huế shootings of 8 May, and Diệm is overthrown and killed in a coup on 1 November.
pointDescs.1965: After a run of coups Nguyễn Cao Kỳ becomes prime minister, and American combat troops arrive in large numbers.
pointDescs.1967: A new constitution grants basic freedoms, and Nguyễn Văn Thiệu is elected president of the Second Republic.
pointDescs.1968: During the Tet Offensive over a million South Vietnamese soldiers are under arms; the offensive fails militarily.
pointDescs.1970: The Land-to-the-Tiller program begins, and US and South Vietnamese forces attack PAVN and Viet Cong bases in Cambodia.
pointDescs.1971: The invasion of North Vietnamese bases in Laos is defeated, a setback for Vietnamization; Thiệu is re-elected unopposed.
pointDescs.1972: The North's conventional invasion in late March is repulsed by October with massive US air support.
pointDescs.1973: At the Paris Peace Accords South Vietnam fields the fourth largest military force in the world, and US aid peaks at $2.3 billion.
pointDescs.1974: Thiệu declares the war restarted, China takes the Paracel Islands, and Congress reduces aid to $700 million.
pointDescs.1975: The Ho Chi Minh Campaign overruns the South, and Dương Văn Minh surrenders unconditionally on 30 April.

Military force established 30 December 1955; the register start 1955 follows the proclamation of 26 October 1955.
